items.prompt_md: A function `f(n)` calls `f(n-1)` and `f(n-2)` and does O(1) other work. How many nodes does its recursion tree have, roughly?
options: About n, since each level has one new value
About 2^n, since each call fans out into two and the tree is about n levels deep
About n^2, since there are two calls per level
About log n, since n shrinks each time
items.answer: About 2^n, since each call fans out into two and the tree is about n levels deep
items.explanation_md: Branching factor 2 over depth about n gives roughly 2^n nodes. It is not n or n^2: the calls multiply, they do not add.

items.prompt_md: What does the *depth* of a recursion tree measure for space complexity?
options: The maximum number of stack frames alive at once, which is extra space even if no arrays are made
The total number of calls ever made
The size of the input only, never extra space
Nothing; the call stack is free memory
items.answer: The maximum number of stack frames alive at once, which is extra space even if no arrays are made
items.explanation_md: Each live call keeps a frame on the call stack, so peak depth is the stack space. Total calls measures time, not space, and the stack is not free.

items.prompt_md: Naive recursive Fibonacci has only n + 1 distinct arguments (0..n) yet takes exponential time. What explains this?
options: Each call does exponential work internally
Python recursion is inherently exponential
Addition of big integers dominates the cost
The same subproblems are recomputed from scratch under many different parents
items.answer: The same subproblems are recomputed from scratch under many different parents
items.explanation_md: The tree keeps re-solving fib(k) for small k. Memoizing turns each distinct argument into a single real computation.

items.prompt_md: After adding a memo dictionary to recursive Fibonacci, what is the time complexity?
options: O(2^n), since memoization does not change the tree
O(log n), since the cache halves the work
O(n), since each of the n + 1 distinct arguments is computed once in O(1)
O(n^2), since each lookup scans the cache
items.answer: O(n), since each of the n + 1 distinct arguments is computed once in O(1)
items.explanation_md: Each distinct argument is computed once and every later visit is a dict lookup. The cache does not scan, and the calls no longer fan out.

items.prompt_md: A recursive function reverses a string by calling itself on `s[1:]` each time. What hidden cost does this add?
options: Nothing; slicing is O(1) in Python
Each slice copies the remaining characters, so total work becomes O(n^2)
It makes the recursion exponential
It reduces the stack depth to log n
items.answer: Each slice copies the remaining characters, so total work becomes O(n^2)
items.explanation_md: `s[1:]` copies n-1, n-2, ... characters across the calls, which sums to O(n^2). Passing indices instead keeps each call O(1).

items.prompt_md: Why can a memoized top-down Fibonacci hit a `RecursionError` for large n while the bottom-up loop does not?
options: Top-down recursion depth grows to about n frames, and Python caps stack depth near 1000 by default
The memo dictionary overflows at 1000 entries
Bottom-up uses more memory so it is safer
Python forbids recursion with a cache
items.answer: Top-down recursion depth grows to about n frames, and Python caps stack depth near 1000 by default
items.explanation_md: Depth n means n live frames, and Python's default limit is about 1000. The loop has no frames to pile up.

items.prompt_md: In the master-theorem intuition for halving recursions, total time is roughly:
options: Work per call multiplied by n
The depth added to the branching factor
The input size divided by the depth
Work per level multiplied by the number of levels
items.answer: Work per level multiplied by the number of levels
items.explanation_md: Sum the work across each level of the tree, then multiply by the number of levels (log n for halving). That is the informal master-theorem recipe.

items.prompt_md: Which statement about the bottom-up Fibonacci loop that keeps only `prev` and `cur` is correct?
options: It is O(1) time because it only keeps two values
It needs O(n) space to remember all earlier values
It reaches the same answer in O(n) time but only O(1) extra space
It is O(2^n) time because it mirrors the recursion
items.answer: It reaches the same answer in O(n) time but only O(1) extra space
items.explanation_md: The loop runs about n iterations, so time is O(n), but it only stores two numbers. Keeping the whole history would cost O(n) space.

items.prompt_md: Binary search written recursively on a sorted array of n items (passing indices, not slices). What are its time and space?
options: O(log n) time and O(1) space
O(log n) time and O(log n) space for the call stack
O(n) time and O(log n) space
O(n log n) time and O(n) space
items.answer: O(log n) time and O(log n) space for the call stack
items.explanation_md: One branch, halving: log n levels of O(1) work. The stack is log n deep, so recursive space is O(log n); the iterative version is O(1).

items.prompt_md: Merge sort halves the array, recurses on both halves, and merges in O(n). What is its time complexity?
options: O(n log n), since each of the log n levels does O(n) total merge work
O(log n), since the array is halved each time
O(n), since each element is merged once
O(n^2), since there are two recursive calls
items.answer: O(n log n), since each of the log n levels does O(n) total merge work
items.explanation_md: Work per level is n (across all nodes on that level) and there are log n levels. Two branches do not make it quadratic because each branch gets half the input.

items.prompt_md: A recursive function `f(n)` makes one call `f(n-1)` and does O(1) other work, with no extra data structures. What is its space complexity?
options: O(1), because no extra data structures are created
O(log n), because n shrinks each call
O(2^n), because recursion always branches
O(n), because the call stack grows n frames deep
items.answer: O(n), because the call stack grows n frames deep
items.explanation_md: Recursion depth is space. One call per level is a line of n frames, so the stack alone is O(n).

items.prompt_md: A recursive function calls itself three times with `n-1` and does O(1) other work. Which is its time complexity?
options: O(3n), since there are three calls
O(n^3), since three calls are made
O(3^n), since the tree has branching factor 3 and depth n
O(n), since the depth is n
items.answer: O(3^n), since the tree has branching factor 3 and depth n
items.explanation_md: Branching factor b over depth n gives b^n nodes. Three calls per node multiplies, not adds, at every level.

items.prompt_md: You must compute the n-th number of a sequence where each term is the sum of the previous two, with n up to 5,000, and want minimal memory.
options: Plain recursion without caching
Iterate upward keeping only the last two values
Build a full table of all n values then read the last
Sort the sequence terms and take the median
items.answer: Iterate upward keeping only the last two values
items.explanation_md: Each term depends on a fixed number of earlier terms, so a rolling window gives O(n) time and O(1) space. Plain recursion is exponential, and a full table wastes O(n) space.

items.prompt_md: A recursive solution recomputes the same (index, remaining) states many times, and there are only about 200 x 200 distinct states.
options: Memoize the recursion (or fill a table bottom-up) over the distinct states
Use a hash set to remove duplicate inputs first
Binary search on the answer
Sort the states by index first
items.answer: Memoize the recursion (or fill a table bottom-up) over the distinct states
items.explanation_md: Overlapping subproblems with few distinct states is the dynamic-programming signature: cache each state so the work is states times per-state cost.

items.prompt_md: You need every ordering of a list of 8 distinct items, and each ordering must be built one choice at a time.
options: Memoize results keyed by list length
Binary search over the possible orderings
Use a monotonic stack to order the items
Backtrack: choose, recurse, then undo the choice
items.answer: Backtrack: choose, recurse, then undo the choice
items.explanation_md: Enumerating all arrangements is a search with choose/explore/un-choose. There are no overlapping subproblems to cache since every path is a distinct output.

items.prompt_md: Given a sorted list of 10^9 numbers in memory (random access), find whether a value is present, as fast as possible.
options: Scan from the left until found
Recurse into both halves and combine results
Binary search: halve the range each step
Build a set of all values first
items.answer: Binary search: halve the range each step
items.explanation_md: A sorted array with direct indexing supports O(log n) halving. Scanning is O(n), and building a set costs O(n) time and memory for one query.

items.prompt_md: Reverse the characters of a string in place, using two indices that move toward each other, with no recursion.
options: Recursion that slices off one character per call
Two pointers swapping from both ends until they meet
Memoize each suffix
Sort the characters descending
items.answer: Two pointers swapping from both ends until they meet
items.explanation_md: Swapping from both ends is O(n) time and O(1) space. Recursion with slicing costs O(n^2) time and O(n) stack.

items.prompt_md: An interviewer says: "Your recursion depth equals n. What happens for n = 10^6?" You need an approach that avoids deep call stacks for a chain-like dependency.
options: Convert to an iterative loop that carries the state forward
Add more recursion to split the work
Use a larger hash map
Sort the input before recursing
items.answer: Convert to an iterative loop that carries the state forward
items.explanation_md: Depth equals stack space and risks a stack overflow. When each step depends only on the previous state, a loop carries that state in O(1) space.

items.prompt_md: Count the number of distinct ways to climb a staircase of n steps taking 1 or 2 steps at a time, n up to 45.
options: Backtrack and list every path, then count them
Binary search on the number of ways
Sort the step sizes and pick greedily
Dynamic programming over step counts, keeping the last two results
items.answer: Dynamic programming over step counts, keeping the last two results
items.explanation_md: Ways(k) = ways(k-1) + ways(k-2) has overlapping subproblems; listing all paths is exponential, and greedy does not count anything.

items.prompt_md: Compute the sum of all node values in a binary tree of n nodes, where each node is visited once.
options: Binary search on node values
Memoize every node's subtree sum
Tree traversal (DFS or BFS), O(n) time, with the tree height driving the stack
Heapify the tree values
items.answer: Tree traversal (DFS or BFS), O(n) time, with the tree height driving the stack
items.explanation_md: A traversal that visits each node once is O(n); recursive DFS stack depth is the tree height. A general tree has no sorted order to binary search.

items.prompt_md: Compute 2 raised to the power n quickly for n up to 10^9 by repeatedly squaring, so the exponent halves each call.
options: Multiply by 2 in a loop n times
Divide the exponent in half each call (fast exponentiation), O(log n)
Memoize every power from 1 to n
Backtrack over all exponent splits
items.answer: Divide the exponent in half each call (fast exponentiation), O(log n)
items.explanation_md: Halving the exponent gives log n levels of O(1) work. A loop of n multiplications is O(n), which is too slow for 10^9.

items.prompt_md: Return the minimum number of coins needed to make an amount up to 10^4, where a naive recursion tries every coin at every step and repeats amounts.
options: Cache the answer per remaining amount (memoization or bottom-up table)
Sort the coins and use binary search on the amount
Backtrack and print every combination
Use a sliding window over the coin list
items.answer: Cache the answer per remaining amount (memoization or bottom-up table)
items.explanation_md: Few distinct amounts with repeated subproblems is a memoization signal: about amount times coins work instead of an exponential tree.
